scenes.contextualRelevance: Explaining the basics of Lewis dot structures for hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, and halogens.

narrativeProgression.description: The woman begins to explain how to draw Lewis dot structures and the preferred structures without using math.
The woman explains that hydrogen forms only one bond and writes a chemical formula for hydrogen on white paper using a black sharpie.

The woman continues to explain that the hydrogen atom will feel like it has two electrons if it shares another electron with another atom and writes a chemical formula for a hydrogen molecule with the number of electrons.
The woman explains that carbon wants to form four bonds and writes a chemical formula for carbon on white paper using a black sharpie.
The woman continues to explain that the carbon atom will feel like it has eight electrons if it shares with other atoms and writes a chemical formula for carbon with the number of electrons.

The woman explains that carbon wants to form four bonds and it could be in the form of four single bonds, or a double bond and two single bonds, or a single bond and a triple bond and writes three types of chemical formulas for carbon.
The woman notes that the compounds found in nature that contain carbon are called organic compounds.
The woman asks what oxygen's Lewis dot structure is and writes a chemical formula for oxygen on white paper using a black sharpie.

The woman explains that oxygen wants to pick up two electrons and when it's covalently bonding to something else, it will form with two bonds and two lone pairs and writes a chemical formula for oxygen with the number of electrons and lone pairs.
The woman continues to explain that oxygen could form two single bonds or a double bond and two lone pairs and writes two chemical formulas for oxygen.
The woman asks to now look at nitrogen and writes a chemical formula for nitrogen on white paper using a black sharpie.

The woman explains that nitrogen wants to pick up three more valence electrons to get an octet of eight electrons to make it stable and writes a chemical formula for nitrogen with the number of electrons.

The woman continues to explain that nitrogen could be in the form of three single bonds or a single bond and a double bond with a lone pair or a nitrogen with a lone pair and a triple bond and writes three chemical formulas for nitrogen.
The woman asks to now look at halogens and writes the label '7A' on white paper using a black sharpie.
The woman notes that halogens are often symbolized with the letter 'X' and writes a chemical formula for a halogen on white paper using a black sharpie.
